statements.virtual-particle-exchange: A force is carried by the exchange of virtual particles, created for a short time in temporary violation of the conservation of mass-energy, as the uncertainty principle allows. Such a particle cannot be observed directly, because observing it would take more time than it exists.
statements.range-and-carrier-mass: A carrier particle can travel only as far as light goes in the time it may exist, $d \approx c\,\Delta t$, and that time is shorter the greater its mass. The heavier the carrier, the shorter the range of the force it carries.
statements.estimate-carrier-mass: The mass of a carrier particle is estimated from the range of its force in three steps: the range gives the time the particle may exist, the uncertainty principle turns that time into an energy, and $\Delta E = mc^{2}$ turns the energy into a mass. The same chain runs backward from a mass to a range.
statements.pions-and-muons: The pions, discovered with about the mass Yukawa predicted, carry the strong force between nucleons; the muon, of nearly the same mass, does not feel the strong force at all.
statements.properties-of-the-four-forces: The four basic forces differ greatly in strength and range: gravity and the electromagnetic force have infinite range, the weak and strong nuclear forces are short ranged, and each is carried by its own particle, the graviton, the photon, the $W^{\pm}$ and $Z^{0}$, and the gluons.
statements.feynman-diagrams: A Feynman diagram is a graph of time against position that shows particles approaching, exchanging virtual particles and leaving.
statements.quantum-electrodynamics: Quantum electrodynamics is the quantum theory of the electromagnetic force, which it treats as carried by virtual photons and calculates from Feynman diagrams. Every later theory of a force is modeled on it.
statements.accelerators-create-matter: A collision can create new particles from its energy, $m = \Delta E/c^{2}$, so the more energy an accelerator gives its particles, the heavier the particles it can create, within the conservation laws.
statements.van-de-graaff-and-cyclotron: The first accelerators were the electrostatic Van de Graaff, which gives particles the energy of a single large voltage, and the cyclotron, which accelerates them across a gap with an alternating voltage of fixed frequency while a magnetic field bends them round again in ever larger circles.
statements.synchrotron: A synchrotron is a circular accelerator in which the frequency of the accelerating voltage and the strength of the magnetic field rise as the particles gain energy, so that they keep to an orbit of fixed radius.
statements.synchrotron-radiation: Synchrotron radiation is the electromagnetic radiation given off by charged particles as a magnetic field bends their path. It costs light particles such as electrons the most energy.
statements.accelerator-gap-voltage: The energy a particle gains across an accelerating gap is $\text{PE}_{\text{elec}} = qV$, so a proton gains 1 eV for each volt it crosses and the energy from a linear accelerator is the sum of its gap voltages.
statements.antimatter-and-annihilation: Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and the opposite charge, and a particle and its antiparticle can annihilate, turning their whole mass into photons that move apart to keep the total momentum zero.
statements.hadrons-and-leptons: Particles are classified first by the forces they feel: hadrons feel the strong nuclear force and leptons do not. Only six leptons exist and they seem fundamental, while the hadrons are many.
statements.bosons-and-fermions: Particles are divided by spin into bosons, with integral spin, and fermions, with half-integral spin, which obey the exclusion principle. All carrier particles are bosons, while quarks and leptons are fermions.
statements.lepton-family-numbers: The six leptons fall into three families, the electron, muon and tau families, and in every reaction the total electron family number $L_{e}$, muon family number $L_{\mu}$ and tau family number $L_{\tau}$ are each conserved.
statements.mesons-and-baryons: The hadrons are of two kinds, told apart not by mass but by decay: a meson can decay to leptons and leave no hadron, while a baryon always decays to another baryon.
statements.baryon-number-conservation: In every reaction the total baryon number is conserved. This is why the proton, the lightest baryon, does not decay, and why the number of nucleons in a nuclear reaction stays the same.
statements.particle-lifetime-and-force: The stronger the force that causes a decay, the faster the decay, so a particle's lifetime shows which force is at work: about $10^{-23}$ s for the strong force and $10^{-10}$ s or longer for the weak force. Leptons among the products also point to the weak force.
statements.strangeness: Strangeness $S$ is a quantum number given to particles to account for decays that every other conservation law allows but that never happen; it is 0 for the ordinary hadrons and nonzero for the strange particles.
statements.check-conservation-in-decays: A decay is checked by adding up the charge, baryon number, lepton family numbers and strangeness before and after: a decay that conserves all of them can happen, and one that changes strangeness can happen only through the weak force.
statements.fundamental-particles: A fundamental particle is one with no substructure and no size beyond its wavelength. The known fundamental particles are of three types: the leptons, the quarks and the carrier particles.
statements.quark-flavors: The flavors are the six kinds of quark: up, down, strange, charm, bottom and top. Their charges are fractions of the proton's, $+\frac{2}{3}q_{e}$ for the up, charm and top quarks and $-\frac{1}{3}q_{e}$ for the down, strange and bottom quarks.
statements.quark-composition-of-hadrons: In the quark model every baryon is made of three quarks and every meson of a quark and an antiquark, rules that give hadrons only integral charges.
statements.quantum-numbers-from-quarks: A hadron's charge, baryon number and strangeness are found by adding those of its quarks, and working backward names the quarks of a particle from its quantum numbers.
statements.weak-force-changes-flavor: The weak force can change the flavor of a quark, and the strong force cannot. Neutron decay is a down quark becoming an up quark, and the same change is why only the weak force can change strangeness.
statements.evidence-for-quarks: No quark has been isolated, yet the evidence for quarks is strong: the $\Omega^{-}$ was found as the quark model predicted, high-energy electrons scatter from three pointlike charges inside the proton, and collisions produce jets of particles from single quarks.
statements.quark-color-and-confinement: Each quark carries one of three colors, and hadrons are always white, a baryon combining three colors and a meson a color and its anticolor. Color lets quarks in states such as $sss$ obey the exclusion principle and explains why a single quark cannot be isolated.
statements.three-families: Leptons, quarks and carrier particles each fall into three analogous families, normal, exotic and more exotic, and the particles of the higher families decay into those of the first.
statements.electroweak-unification: Electroweak theory unifies the electromagnetic and weak forces, showing them to be one force at high energy. It predicted the $W^{\pm}$ and $Z^{0}$ and their masses before they were found.
statements.gluons-and-qcd: Eight gluons carry the strong force between quarks and can change their color. Pion exchange between nucleons is, underneath, the exchange of quarks and gluons.
statements.standard-model: The Standard Model is the combination of electroweak theory and quantum chromodynamics, the present theory of the fundamental particles and forces, with the Higgs boson its last predicted piece.
statements.grand-unified-theories: A grand unified theory unifies the strong force with the electroweak force. Higher energy probes smaller distances, and at extremely high energies the strengths of the forces come together, far beyond the reach of any accelerator.
statements.proton-decay: Grand unified theories predict that the proton decays, as in $p \to \pi^{0} + e^{+}$, with a lifetime near $10^{31}$ y. Proton decay has not been observed, which constrains the theories.

new.name: Virtual particle
new.statement: A virtual particle is a particle created for a short time in temporary violation of the conservation of mass-energy, as the uncertainty principle allows, and which cannot be observed directly.

new.name: Pion
new.statement: A pion is the particle exchanged between nucleons that carries the strong nuclear force; it is a meson with a mass about 270 times the electron's.

new.name: Meson
new.statement: A meson is a hadron that can decay to leptons and leave no hadron; it is made of a quark and an antiquark. The first mesons found had masses between those of the electron and the proton.

new.name: Gluon
new.statement: A gluon is one of eight massless particles that carry the strong force between quarks.

new.name: Van de Graaff accelerator
new.statement: A Van de Graaff is an electrostatic accelerator that gives charged particles the energy of the single large voltage it builds up on a charged dome.

new.name: Cyclotron
new.statement: A cyclotron is an accelerator in which a magnetic field bends charged particles in a spiral while an alternating voltage of fixed frequency accelerates them each time they cross the gap between two hollow D-shaped electrodes.

new.name: Linear accelerator
new.statement: A linear accelerator accelerates charged particles in a straight line through a series of tubes, giving them energy across the gap between each tube and the next.

new.name: Boson
new.statement: A boson is a particle with integral spin, 0, 1, 2 and so on; bosons do not obey the Pauli exclusion principle.

new.name: Fermion
new.statement: A fermion is a particle with half-integral spin, 1/2, 3/2 and so on; fermions obey the Pauli exclusion principle.

new.name: Hadron
new.statement: A hadron is a particle that feels the strong nuclear force.

new.name: Lepton
new.statement: A lepton is a fundamental particle that does not feel the strong nuclear force; the six leptons are the electron, muon and tau and their three neutrinos.

new.name: Baryon
new.statement: A baryon is a hadron that always decays to another baryon; it is made of three quarks.

new.name: Baryon number $B$
new.statement: Baryon number $B$ is a quantum number equal to $+1$ for a baryon, $-1$ for an antibaryon and 0 for mesons and leptons.

new.name: Electron family number $L_{e}$
new.statement: The electron family number $L_{e}$ is $+1$ for the electron and its neutrino, $-1$ for their antiparticles and 0 for every other particle.

new.name: Muon family number $L_{\mu}$
new.statement: The muon family number $L_{\mu}$ is $+1$ for the muon and its neutrino, $-1$ for their antiparticles and 0 for every other particle.

new.name: Tau family number $L_{\tau}$
new.statement: The tau family number $L_{\tau}$ is $+1$ for the tau and its neutrino, $-1$ for their antiparticles and 0 for every other particle.

new.name: Conservation of total muon family number
new.statement: In every reaction the total muon family number is conserved.

new.name: Strangeness is conserved by the strong force, not the weak
new.statement: Strangeness is conserved in reactions caused by the strong and electromagnetic forces but can change in reactions caused by the weak force.

new.name: Up quark $u$
new.statement: The up quark is the quark flavor of charge $+\frac{2}{3}q_{e}$ in the first family; the proton is $uud$.

new.name: Down quark $d$
new.statement: The down quark is the quark flavor of charge $-\frac{1}{3}q_{e}$ in the first family; the neutron is $udd$.

new.name: Strange quark $s$
new.statement: The strange quark is the quark flavor of charge $-\frac{1}{3}q_{e}$ and strangeness $-1$ in the second family.

new.name: Charm quark $c$
new.statement: The charm quark is the quark flavor of charge $+\frac{2}{3}q_{e}$ in the second family.

new.name: Bottom quark $b$
new.statement: The bottom quark is the quark flavor of charge $-\frac{1}{3}q_{e}$ in the third family.

new.name: Top quark $t$
new.statement: The top quark is the quark flavor of charge $+\frac{2}{3}q_{e}$ in the third family, by far the heaviest quark.

new.name: Color
new.statement: Color is a quantum number of quarks, with three values called red, green and blue, and their anticolors for antiquarks; it has nothing to do with visible color.

new.name: Quark confinement
new.statement: The theory of quark confinement holds that the force between quarks grows with their separation, so a single quark can never be isolated and quarks are found only in white combinations.

new.name: Quantum chromodynamics
new.statement: Quantum chromodynamics is the theory of the strong force between quarks, carried by gluons and acting on the quarks' color.

new.name: Higgs boson
new.statement: The Higgs boson is a massive particle predicted by the Standard Model to explain why the other particles have mass, and found in 2012.
